How several mappings of one action combine (UE5
EInputActionAccumulationBehavior). TakeHighest keeps, per axis, the value
with the largest magnitude, so a stick at 0.5 and a key at 1 read 1 rather
than clamping a sum; Cumulative adds them, so opposite keys cancel.

members.name: TouchContact
members.doc:
Touch (M4.5): `touchIndex` picks the contact slot (0 = first finger
down). Contact is the button analogue (1 while the slot is live —
Tap/Hold triggers compose on top), Position feeds absolute
window-pixel coordinates, Delta is the per-frame movement — the touch
twin of MouseDeltaX/Y for drag-to-look. Serialized by the IMC asset
path; the legacy per-device-array config predates touch and stays
keyboard/mouse/gamepad-only.

types.name: InputActionSystem
types.doc:
Singleton that evaluates input actions each frame based on raw InputManager state.
Manages a stack of InputContexts with priority ordering.

members.doc:
The process-wide instance: player 0 (keyboard, mouse and every pad the
bindings name) and every single-player game.

members.name: CreatePlayerInstance
members.signature: static std::unique_ptr<InputActionSystem> CreatePlayerInstance(InputManager* inputManager, int32_t gamepadIndex, bool keyboardMouse)
members.doc:
One more local player's own instance (split-screen co-op). It owns its
context stack, trigger state and rebinds, and reads only the devices it
is routed to: every gamepad binding reads `gamepadIndex` whatever pad
the binding names (so one mapping context serves every player), and
keyboard / mouse bindings read nothing unless `keyboardMouse`. The
contexts the global instance holds right now are copied in.

members.doc:
Push a context onto the stack, inserted by InputContext::GetPriority

priorities keep push order).

members.name: PopContext
members.doc:
Remove a context from the stack (does not destroy it). Its actions are
cancel-evaluated so nothing resumes from stale mid-episode state on the
next push (a held Tap would otherwise fire on re-push's first release).

project tier declared alongside the mapping-context assets that
supersede it — cannot produce input, so its bindings cannot collide
with anything.

members.name: GetDebugSnapshot

members.name: IsDebugOverlayEnabled
members.doc:

members.name: MouseSensitivity
members.doc:
Player look preferences, backed by `i.MouseSensitivity` and
`i.MouseInvertY` and applied to both mouse-delta sources before any
binding modifier — a game that ships several look actions gets them on
all of them, and a mapping context authored without them cannot opt the
player out by omission. Sensitivity is clamped to 0.05..10 because a zero
is a dead mouse the player cannot undo from inside the game.

One player-authored rebind: the complete binding list a player chose for a
single action in a single context. The user tier stores overrides rather
than a snapshot of every context, because the Enhanced-Input contexts are

members.doc: If true, this context blocks lower-priority contexts from receiving input

members.name: SetPriority
members.doc:
Stack ordering weight: InputActionSystem::PushContext inserts so the
stack stays sorted ascending, back = highest = evaluated first. Equal
priorities keep push order (a later push lands above earlier equals),
which preserves the legacy "push means top" behaviour at the default 0.

members.name: SetRuntimeOnly
members.doc:
Runtime-only contexts are rebuilt from other data every session (the
Enhanced-Input subsystem mirrors IMC assets into synthetic contexts).
SaveBindings skips them — persisting one would boot a phantom copy that
shadows the real asset next session.

types.name: EInputMode
types.doc:
UE-style input routing. Set by gameplay (SetInputMode) when a UI modal
opens/closes; the platform event pump consults it — together with the
per-event "did the UI consume this?" flag — to decide whether a device
event reaches the gameplay subsystems.
GameOnly   — UI ignores input, game receives everything.
GameAndUI  — both receive input, but events the UI consumed (a click on
a button, a keypress in a text field) are withheld from the
game so mouse-look doesn't turn behind an open widget.
UIOnly     — UI receives input, the game receives nothing.

types.name: EInputDevice
types.doc:
The physical device the player most recently used. Lets a HUD pick the
right button-prompt glyphs (keyboard keycaps vs. Xbox vs. PlayStation).
The glyph art is the game's; this only tracks which family to show.

members.name: AssignGamepadSlot
members.doc:
Explicit player-slot assignment. Without it the first pad plugged in is
always player 1, so a couch session cannot put the host's pad on slot 2
without re-plugging in the right order. Swaps the pad in currentSlot
with whatever occupies newSlot (state, native handle and family move
with it) and remembers the choice per device id in the user file, so
the next connect of that hardware lands in the same slot.

members.name: OnKeyDown
members.doc:
Event handlers - called by Window.

When a recording is active the On* call forwards to the recorder before
touching the subsystem. When a playback is active the On* call is
*suppressed* — real OS events get dropped on the floor for the duration
of the replay so they can't pollute the recorded state. The playback
re-enters these same sinks via an internal "injecting" flag that
bypasses both gates so injected events still reach the subsystems and
never re-record.

members.name: InjectKeyDown
members.doc:
Synthetic input for tests, automation and accessibility tooling. An
injected event lands in the device subsystems exactly like a replayed
one: it bypasses the playback suppression gate and the UI-consumed
gate, and is never recorded (a recording should capture the user, not
the harness driving them).

members.name: ResetDeviceStateOnFocusLoss
members.doc:
Focus loss: the OS never delivers key-ups for keys held across an
Alt-Tab, so every held key/button gets a synthetic release through the
normal Up sinks (releases are never suppressed and triggers see a real
Completed edge), and axes/deltas zero. Without this the character
walks into a wall forever after a focus switch mid-WASD.

members.name: GetFocusLossSerial
members.doc:
Bumped by every focus-loss reset. Anything that latches key state
OUTSIDE the device bitsets (the editor fly camera keeps its own WASD
flags) polls this once a frame and drops its latches when it moves —
the OS never sends those key-ups either.

members.name: SetInputMode
members.doc:
Gameplay sets the input mode when a menu opens/closes. The platform event
pump sets the per-event "UI consumed this" flag from the UI layer's
return value BEFORE forwarding the event to the On* sinks below;
those sinks then drop the event for gameplay when
IsGameInputSuppressed() is true. Device tracking (below) still
updates regardless — a suppressed gamepad press still means the
player is on a gamepad.

members.name: SetUIConsumedCurrentEvent
members.doc:
"consumed" means the UI ACTED on this one event — a widget handled it,
a modal or menu owned it, or the focused widget swallowed it. It must
never mean "something is focused": a HUD button that keeps focus after
a click would then suppress every key the game reads for as long as it
holds it. The resulting policy, per event class:

key down / character   suppressed only when the UI took THAT key, so
a focused text box eats typing and nothing else
key up / button up     never suppressed (the Up sinks ignore the gate),
or a key held into a focus change stays down
mouse button down      suppressed only when a widget handled the press;
a click nobody took reaches the game
mouse motion / wheel   suppressed only while a widget is dragging or
scrolling with it, so mouse look survives a
cursor resting over the HUD
gamepad                the UI layer never sees pad events, so only
EInputMode::UIOnly withholds them

members.name: GetLastInputDevice
members.doc:
Updated on every device event so a HUD can query which button-prompt
family to show. The gamepad *family* (Xbox / PlayStation / Nintendo /
generic) is resolved by the platform layer on connect and pushed via
SetGamepadKind; per-slot until then it is GamepadGeneric.

members.name: SetGamepadKind
members.doc:
Physical index (Window calls it on connect); the family lands on the
logical slot the pad resolves to.

members.name: SetCursorLockRequested
members.doc:
Cursor lock request (for FPS-style mouse capture)
Game code calls these, engine applies them each frame.

The "user escaped" sticky flag (set by NotifyUserEscapedLock when
ESC fires) overrides game intent — even if a script calls this
every Update, the engine won't re-engage the lock until the user
*clicks* in the window (Unity-style "ESC frees, click re-locks").
Setting lock=false from game code clears the escape too, so a
hand-off between scripts works naturally.

members.name: IsCursorLockSuppressedByEscape
members.doc:
Engine-internal: sync pass uses this to decide whether to actually
engage. While true, ignore m_wantCursorLock.

members.name: NotifyUserEscapedLock
members.doc:
ESC handler calls this — locks out re-engagement until the user
clicks in the window or game code does an explicit lock=false
→ lock=true cycle.

members.name: NotifyUserClicked
members.doc:
Mouse click clears the escape — the next sync re-engages if the
game still wants the lock. Window calls this on any button-down.

A click the UI took is not the click this means. In a non-modal pause
screen — the default — the first press on a menu button re-engaged the
lock, the cursor went back to relative mode, and the menu could not be
clicked again.

members.name: SetCursorVisible
members.doc: Cursor visibility (separate from lock)

members.name: GetCursorConfineMode
members.doc:
The mode the sync pass should honour: the i.CursorConfine override when
it is set, else what game code asked for.

members.name: ShouldConfineCursor
members.signature: static bool ShouldConfineCursor(ECursorConfine mode, bool windowFocused, bool cursorLocked)
members.doc:
What the engine's sync pass should apply this frame. Focus is a hard
gate in every mode: confining a cursor the user has alt-tabbed away from
is how an application stops being closable.

members.name: EndInputFrame
members.doc:
Engine hook — called once per frame after Update() + window event pump
+ SetMouseDelta so the recorder's frame marker bundles every event from
*this* frame. No-op when not recording.

types.name: InputManager::ECursorConfine
types.doc:
Cursor confinement (separate from BOTH).

The lock above takes the cursor into relative mode, which confines it as
a side effect — so a mouse-look game was covered and nothing else was. A
game that keeps a VISIBLE cursor (a strategy camera, a twin-stick, a
drag across an inventory) had no way to stop that cursor leaving the
window, and in windowed mode on two monitors the next click lands in
another application. UE calls this the mouse LOCK MODE; this is the same
axis, named for what it does.

members.name: Never
members.doc: the cursor may leave the window

members.name: WhileCaptured
members.doc: only while the game holds the cursor lock (relative mode confines anyway — this just makes it explicit)

members.name: Always
members.doc: confine whenever the window has focus, visible cursor included

types.name: InputPlayback
types.doc:
Reads a .mirec file produced by InputRecorder and replays its events into
InputManager one frame at a time. The full event stream is read into a
std::vector at Load() time — recordings are small (KB to single-digit MB
for long sessions), so streaming from disk during gameplay would only add
hitch risk for no real memory win.

members.name: Load
members.doc:
Loads `path` into memory and parses the header. Returns false if the
file can't be opened, is shorter than the header, or has wrong magic /
unsupported version. On failure the playback is left inactive so a
subsequent Load() can retry.

members.name: Stop
members.doc: Aborts playback. Safe to call when not active.

members.name: IsFinished
members.doc:
True when the read cursor has reached the end of the stream. Hosts can
poll this to auto-stop or loop. Becomes true after the last frame's
events have been injected by InjectFrame().
True once the stream ended for ANY reason — natural end-of-data OR an
abort (truncated file, unknown tag). The old m_active gate made an
aborted playback read as never-finished, and hosts looping on
!IsFinished() hung forever.

members.name: InjectFrame
members.doc:
Replays every event up to and including the next FrameMarker into the
given InputManager. Each call advances exactly one recorded frame —
matched 1:1 with InputManager::Update(). When the stream is finished
becomes a no-op (so a stuck playback won't crash the game loop).

types.name: InputRecorder
types.doc:
Captures raw input events into an in-memory buffer and flushes the buffer
to disk on Stop(). Buffering avoids any file-I/O cost during gameplay — a
10-minute session at 60 fps with heavy input is well under 10 MB so the
memory pressure is negligible. The recorder is owned by InputManager and
receives forwarded events from the public On* sinks.

Frame boundaries are explicit: InputManager calls EndFrame() once per game
frame, which writes a FrameMarker into the stream. The marker is what
playback uses to advance frame-by-frame, so missing one collapses two
recorded frames into one on replay.

members.name: Start
members.doc:
Starts buffering. Returns false if `outputPath` resolves to a directory
that doesn't exist (we don't auto-create). Existing files are silently
overwritten on Stop().

members.name: Stop
members.doc:
Flushes the buffer to disk. Safe to call when not recording (no-op).
Returns true if a file was written (i.e. Start() had been called).

members.name: FrameCount
members.doc:
Frame counter incremented each EndFrame(). 0 before the first marker is
written, so the count matches "number of frames fully captured".

members.name: OnKeyDown
members.doc:
Event sinks — called by InputManager when this recorder is active.
All record raw values, untouched (e.g. mouse positions stay in pixels,
gamepad axes are pre-deadzone). Playback re-injects via the same sinks.

types.name: InputRecordingHeader
types.doc:
On-disk format for recorded input streams (.mirec).

Header (56 bytes) followed by a stream of tagged events. Events that share a
frame are written sequentially; a FrameMarker byte separates frames. The
first frame has no leading marker — the marker is a "frame N just ended"
signal, not a "frame N starts here" one. Recording stops after the final
frame marker is written, so playback knows the stream is complete.

All multi-byte fields are little-endian. The format is host-portable in
theory but in practice only x86_64 / arm64 little-endian is exercised.

members.name: magic
members.doc: "MIRP"

members.name: version
members.doc: currently 1

members.name: frameCount
members.doc: number of FrameMarker events

members.name: eventCount
members.doc: events excluding markers

members.name: reserved
members.doc: zero — leaves room for future header fields

types.name: InputEventType
types.doc:
Tag byte for each event. Frame marker is 0xFF (sentinel) so a corrupt /
truncated file is easy to detect — readers will see a malformed payload
before they trip a marker.

types.name: TouchPhase
types.doc:
Lifecycle of a touch point. Each finger transitions:
None → Began → (Moved | Stationary)* → (Ended | Canceled) → removed

"Stationary" is synthesised by Update() — SDL only sends down / motion / up,
so any touch that didn't receive a motion event this frame is downgraded
from Moved/Began to Stationary at the start of the next frame.

types.name: TouchPoint
types.doc:
Single finger contact. Coordinates are in **window pixels** (already
multiplied by window size) so game code doesn't have to know about SDL's
normalised 0..1 finger coordinates. Delta is the per-frame movement vector
(also in pixels).

members.name: fingerId
members.doc: SDL finger ID (stable per touch)

members.name: dx
members.doc: movement since previous frame

members.name: pressure
members.doc: 0..1 if hardware reports it, else 1

types.name: TouchInput
types.doc:
Per-frame touch state. SDL events arrive between Update() calls; Update()
folds them into a stable snapshot and drops Ended/Canceled entries so each
frame sees only currently-active contacts plus their final-frame Ended
states.

members.name: OnFingerDown
members.signature: void OnFingerDown(uint64_t fingerId, float x, float y, float pressure)
members.doc:
Called by InputManager / Window from SDL_EVENT_FINGER_* handlers.
x/y are pixel coordinates (window space), already converted from SDL's
normalised 0..1 by the caller. SDL doesn't emit Stationary — that's
synthesised internally.

members.name: Update
members.doc:
Called once per frame **before** event polling — promotes Began/Moved →
Stationary, drops Ended/Canceled. Window's ProcessMessages runs polling
immediately after this, so the new SDL events overwrite the synthesised
Stationary phase for any finger that actually moved.

members.name: GetActiveTouches
members.doc:
Active touches snapshot for the current frame. Includes Ended/Canceled
entries for the single frame they fired in — gameplay can detect a
release without missing it.

members.name: GetTouchByFingerId
members.doc: Lookup by SDL finger ID — returns nullptr if not active this frame.

members.name: GetTouch
members.doc:
Lookup by zero-based index (for `for (int i = 0; i < TouchCount(); ++i)`
iteration in scripting languages without iterator support).
